title: King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
setting: A pre-Christian Britain of dukedoms and earldoms, moving from a palace to open heath and finally to the cliffs and camps around Dover
lengthNote: Around 3,300 lines in a conflated text; the quarto and the Folio each contain several hundred lines the other lacks
openingLine: I thought the king had more affected the Duke of Albany than Cornwall.
summary: An old king asks his three daughters to say how much they love him, and disinherits the one who will not perform. Within two acts he has no soldiers, no roof and no title, and the play spends the next three watching what is left of a man when the offices are taken away. A second family repeats the mistake with sons, and by the end both fathers have learned to see and neither survives the knowledge.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of King Lear
sourceText.note: The Globe numbering follows a conflated text. The 1608 quarto and the 1623 Folio differ in hundreds of readings, and the Folio omits a whole scene that many editions print as 4.3.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After Harsnett's Declaration of 1603, which supplied Edgar's fiends, and before the recorded court performance of 1606.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: As a True Chronicle Historie, printed for Nathaniel Butter; the Folio of 1623 calls it a tragedy.

atAGlance.label: Two early texts
atAGlance.note: The Folio adds more than a hundred lines and drops around three hundred. Editors must choose, conflate or print both.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two full plots — Lear's daughters and Gloucester's sons — running in parallel and colliding on the heath.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A ceremony that cannot be undone
structure.summary: Lear turns the handover of a kingdom into a public competition in flattery, and punishes the one daughter who declines to compete. The same act shows Edmund forging a letter and persuading his father of the opposite of the truth. Both fathers act on speech alone, and both are wrong within a hundred lines of hearing it.

scenes.title: The love test
scenes.summary: Cordelia says nothing, is disinherited and married to France; Kent objects and is banished.

scenes.title: The forged letter
scenes.summary: Edmund persuades Gloucester that Edgar plots against him, using a document he wrote himself.

scenes.title: Goneril's instructions
scenes.summary: She tells her steward to treat the old king and his knights coldly on purpose.

scenes.title: A hundred knights
scenes.summary: Kent returns in disguise, the Fool arrives, and Lear curses Goneril with sterility.

scenes.title: Leaving for Regan
scenes.summary: The Fool works on Lear's mistake; Lear names the fear that will occupy the rest of the play.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The retinue is bargained down to nothing
structure.summary: Edmund stages an attack on himself and inherits his brother's place. Kent is put in the stocks — an insult to the king through his servant — and Lear arrives to find the two sisters auctioning his household downwards from a hundred knights to none. He walks out into weather rather than accept the last offer.

scenes.title: Edmund's wound
scenes.summary: A staged skirmish sends Edgar into flight and makes Edmund the loyal son.

scenes.title: Kent in the stocks
scenes.summary: A servant of the king is punished by a duke, and Gloucester's protest is overruled.

scenes.title: Poor Tom
scenes.summary: Edgar decides that the only safe identity left to him is that of a mad beggar.

scenes.title: What need one?
scenes.summary: The sisters reduce the retinue by arithmetic; Lear goes out into the storm.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Weather, and a mock trial in a hovel
structure.summary: Lear shouts at the elements, then does something he has never done before: he thinks about people who have no shelter on any night of the year. The scenes alternate between the heath and Gloucester's castle, so the king's disintegration is cut against the machinery of a coup, and the act ends with a duke pulling out an old man's eyes in his own house.

scenes.title: News of France
scenes.summary: Kent tells a gentleman of the division between the dukes and of forces landing.

scenes.title: The storm
scenes.summary: Lear commands the weather, and the Fool answers him in riddles and rhyme.

scenes.title: Gloucester's secret
scenes.summary: He confides his loyalty to the king to the son who immediately reports it.

scenes.title: The hovel
scenes.summary: Lear meets Poor Tom, and tears off his own clothes to match him.

scenes.title: The betrayal rewarded
scenes.summary: Edmund is made Earl of Gloucester for the information he has just given.

scenes.title: The mock trial
scenes.summary: Lear arraigns a joint-stool as Goneril before a beggar, a fool and a disguised earl.

scenes.title: The blinding
scenes.summary: Cornwall puts out Gloucester's eyes; a servant kills him for it and is killed.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Two ruined fathers, one led and one found
structure.summary: A blind man is guided towards a cliff by the son he disowned, and survives a fall that never happens. A mad king wanders through a field preaching about justice to a man with no eyes. The act ends with the one scene of repair the play allows: Cordelia's army has landed, and Lear wakes up in clean clothes not sure whether he is dead.

scenes.title: Led by Poor Tom
scenes.summary: Gloucester asks a beggar to take him to Dover, not knowing he has hired his son.

scenes.title: Albany turns
scenes.summary: Albany names his wife a fiend; news arrives of Cornwall's death.

scenes.title: Cordelia's grief reported
scenes.summary: A gentleman describes how she received the letters — a scene the Folio does not print.

scenes.title: The search
scenes.summary: Cordelia sends a hundred soldiers to find her father in the high-grown corn.

scenes.title: Regan's jealousy
scenes.summary: Regan interrogates Oswald about Goneril's letters to Edmund.

scenes.title: The cliff at Dover
scenes.summary: The fall that is not a fall, then Lear crowned with weeds on justice, authority and adultery.

scenes.title: Waking
scenes.summary: Lear comes back to himself, kneels to Cordelia, and asks her to forget and forgive.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The battle is won by the wrong side of the argument
structure.summary: The British army defeats the French, so the reunion of Act IV lasts one scene. Edmund's counter-order for Cordelia's death outlives the duel that kills him, by minutes. The play refuses to convert any of this into consolation: the last thing Lear does is ask five people to look at his daughter's lips.

scenes.title: Before the battle
scenes.summary: Edmund calculates between two sisters; Edgar delivers a letter to Albany.

scenes.title: The defeat
scenes.summary: Lear and Cordelia are taken; Edgar tells his father that ripeness is all.

scenes.title: The end
scenes.summary: Prison, a challenge, a duel, two dead sisters, a reprieve too late, and Lear with Cordelia's body.

characters.name: King Lear
characters.summary: A man who has never in his life been contradicted and cannot tell the difference between love and the language of love. What the play takes from him is not power — he gives that away in the first scene — but the assumptions that came with it, and what is left underneath turns out to be capable of pity for the first time at eighty.
characters.clue: He asks three women to say how much they love him, and ends the play carrying the one who refused.

characters.name: Cordelia
characters.summary: She speaks about a hundred lines in the whole play and is absent from the middle three acts, which is part of the design: the play keeps taking her away. Her refusal in the first scene is not defiance but an unwillingness to price a relationship, and it costs her a kingdom in under fifty lines.
characters.clue: Asked to bid for a third of a kingdom, she offers a word that means nothing, and is believed.

characters.name: Goneril
characters.role: Lear's eldest daughter, Duchess of Albany
characters.summary: She wins the first scene by saying what is wanted and spends the rest of the play being right about her father's knights and wrong about everything else. The play gives her a real grievance and then lets her overrun it: by Act IV she is poisoning her sister and writing to a man about killing her husband.
characters.clue: She tells her steward to grow cold to the old man on purpose, and later poisons her own sister.

characters.name: Regan
characters.role: Lear's second daughter, Duchess of Cornwall
characters.summary: She follows her sister's lead in Act I and outruns her afterwards. It is Regan who suggests plucking out the second eye, and Regan who kills the servant who objects. Widowed in the same scene, she immediately begins competing for Edmund, and dies of her sister's poison without ever suspecting it.
characters.clue: She asks what need her father has of even one attendant, and later calls for the other eye.

characters.name: Earl of Gloucester
characters.role: Lear's courtier, father of Edgar and Edmund
characters.summary: He jokes about his illegitimate son's conception in the play's opening exchange and never notices that the son is listening. His plot rhymes with Lear's without repeating it: Lear cannot read speech, Gloucester cannot read a document, and it is Gloucester who is punished physically for a loyalty he only just found the nerve to act on.
characters.clue: He believes a forged letter, loses both eyes in his own house, and asks a beggar to lead him to a cliff.

characters.name: Edmund
characters.summary: The only character who tells the audience his plan and keeps to it. He argues that the law's distinction between his brother and himself is arbitrary, which is true, and then uses the point to justify anything at all. His attempt to do one good thing arrives about ninety seconds too late to save Cordelia.
characters.clue: He forges a letter in his brother's hand, cuts his own arm to prove his loyalty, and is loved by two sisters at once.

characters.name: Edgar
characters.summary: He is tricked out of his name in Act I and spends four acts wearing other people's, of which Poor Tom is only the first. His care for his father is real and strangely cruel — he lets Gloucester believe in a miracle rather than tell him who is holding his arm — and he ends the play holding a kingdom nobody would want.
characters.clue: He blackens his face, takes the name of a Bedlam beggar, and leads his blind father to a cliff that is not there.

characters.name: Earl of Kent
characters.role: Lear's banished servant, disguised as Caius
characters.summary: He contradicts the king to his face in the first scene, is banished for it, and comes back in disguise the same week to carry on doing the job. His loyalty is not sentimental: he trips Oswald, insults Cornwall and gets himself locked in the stocks. At the end he declines the kingdom because he has an appointment elsewhere.
characters.clue: Banished for telling the truth, he shaves his beard, changes his voice and takes service with the man who banished him.

characters.name: The Fool
characters.summary: He arrives after Cordelia leaves and vanishes after the mock trial, which has made some readers connect them. His jokes are all one joke, repeated until it stops being funny: you gave away the thing that made you worth obeying. He is the only person allowed to say it, and he keeps saying it through the worst of the weather.
characters.clue: He tells the king that he is an O without a figure, and disappears from the play after a trial held in a hovel.

themes.name: Nothing, and the price of language
themes.summary: The word runs through both plots like a fault line: Cordelia's answer, Lear's reply, Edmund's 'nothing' as he pockets a forged letter, the Fool's arithmetic of noughts. The play sets speech that performs feeling against speech that measures it, and shows a state making irreversible decisions on the strength of the first.
themes.development: A refusal in 1.1, a joke through Act I, a fact by Act III, when Lear has nothing left to compare with, and an answer in 5.3 where a father asks a dead daughter to speak.

themes.name: Sight, blindness and judgement
themes.summary: Kent tells Lear to see better in the first scene, and the play spends five acts taking the metaphor literally. Gloucester says he stumbled when he saw; Lear, mad, tells a blind man that a man may see how this world goes with no eyes. Understanding in this play is consistently something that arrives after the organ of understanding has been destroyed.
themes.development: Figurative in Act I, appallingly literal in 3.7, and reversed in 4.6, where the blind man and the mad king conduct the play's clearest analysis of power.

themes.name: Nature and the unnatural
themes.summary: Everyone in the play appeals to nature and they mean incompatible things by it. Lear calls on it to make his daughter sterile; Edmund makes it his goddess and means appetite without law; Gloucester reads it in eclipses. The storm is the argument brought on stage, and it answers nobody.
themes.development: Invoked as authority in Acts I and II, unanswering in Act III, and reduced in 3.4 to a bare forked animal with nothing owed to it.

themes.name: Justice and authority
themes.summary: The play holds two trials. The first is a mock one in a hovel, where a madman arraigns a stool; the second is a duel between brothers decided by force. In between, Lear works out that a dog is obeyed in office and that the difference between the justice and the thief is a change of places — the most radical political speech Shakespeare ever gives a king.
themes.development: Ceremonial in 1.1, parodied in 3.6, dismantled in 4.6, and finally left to a chivalric combat that settles a private quarrel and saves nobody.

themes.name: Age, need and dependence
themes.summary: The quarrel that drives Lear onto the heath is about a number: a hundred knights, then fifty, then twenty-five, then what need one. The daughters' case is not obviously wrong, and the play knows it. What Lear finds in answer is that need is not the measure of a life, an argument he can only make once he has lost the argument.
themes.development: Negotiated downwards through Act II, answered in 2.4, and turned outwards in 3.4, where the same reasoning is applied to people who never had anything to lose.

themes.name: Service and loyalty
themes.summary: The play's decency is almost entirely in its servants. Kent takes a beating for a master who sacked him; an unnamed servant of Cornwall's draws a sword to stop a blinding and dies for it; an old tenant leads Gloucester when his family cannot. Rank organises the tragedy, but obligation runs the other way.
themes.development: Punished in 2.2, fatal in 3.7, and finally the only bond left standing in 5.3, where Kent follows his master out of the play.

techniques.name: The double plot
techniques.definition: Two parallel stories staged so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Shakespeare's only tragedy with a fully developed subplot: Lear misreads speech, Gloucester misreads a document, and the two ruined fathers meet in 4.6 so that the comparison happens on stage rather than in the reader's head.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Language that reduces people to beasts, appetite or prey.
techniques.inThisBook: Pelicans, kites, wolves, serpent's teeth, a dog obeyed in office, and finally the bare forked animal: the play measures how far a person can be stripped by how much animal vocabulary is used about them.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character adopting another identity in full view of the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Kent and Edgar are both disguised for most of the play, and both keep the secret from the people it would comfort — Edgar's refusal to tell his father who he is turns a convention of comedy into an act of prolonged, well-meant cruelty.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Shifting between metre and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.inThisBook: Lear's verse breaks down into prose on the heath and in the Dover fields, so the collapse can be heard before it is stated; the Fool works almost entirely in prose and rhyme.

techniques.name: The storm as antagonist
techniques.definition: Weather staged as an active force rather than a background.
techniques.inThisBook: Lear addresses the storm directly, commands it, and then concedes that it owes him nothing — a three-stage argument with the sky that no amount of thunder machinery can win for him.

techniques.name: Riddle and aside
techniques.definition: Speech aimed past its apparent hearer, at the audience or at nobody.
techniques.inThisBook: The Fool's riddles say to the theatre what nobody at court may say to the king; Edgar's asides during 4.1 let the audience hold a piece of knowledge that would change everything if it were spoken aloud.

quotations.text: Unhappy that I am, I cannot heave My heart into my mouth: I love your majesty According to my bond; nor more nor less.
quotations.speaker: Cordelia
quotations.context: Her explanation after answering the love test with a single word.
quotations.analysis: 'Bond' is a legal term, and she uses it deliberately: she is offering an obligation that can be relied on instead of a quantity that cannot be checked. 'Nor more nor less' is the sentence her father hears as coldness and the play treats as the only honest accounting in the scene.

quotations.text: Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: After Cordelia has twice said 'Nothing'.
quotations.analysis: He states a law of physics and applies it to affection, which is exactly the category error the play is about. The second half of the line is the important half: he gives her another turn, so the disaster that follows is not a misunderstanding but a decision taken with a chance to reconsider.

quotations.text: See better, Lear; and let me still remain The true blank of thine eye.
quotations.speaker: Kent
quotations.context: Refusing to leave after being told to get out of the king's sight.
quotations.analysis: The blank is the white centre of an archery target, so Kent is asking to be the thing his master aims at — a servant volunteering to be a mark. He also drops the royal address and uses the king's name, which in this court is the offence.

quotations.text: Thou, nature, art my goddess; to thy law My services are bound. Wherefore should I Stand in the plague of custom, and permit The curiosity of nations to deprive me,
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: The opening of his first soliloquy, holding the letter he has just forged.
quotations.analysis: He borrows the vocabulary of service and law and points it at a goddess who has neither. The argument about primogeniture is genuinely good — an accident of birth order and marriage decides everything about him — which is why the play lets him make it before it lets him act on it.

quotations.text: Now, gods, stand up for bastards!
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: The closing line of the soliloquy, as Gloucester comes in.
quotations.analysis: A prayer shouted at the top of an exit line, immediately before the trick it asks help with begins. The word he has just spent twenty lines objecting to is the one he plants at the end for emphasis, which tells you he intends to keep it rather than escape it.

quotations.text: Who is it that can tell me who I am?
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: In Goneril's house, finding that his own knights are being treated as an inconvenience.
quotations.analysis: The Fool answers 'Lear's shadow', and the answer is exact: without the retinue, the ceremony and the obedience, there is no test he can apply to himself. The question is asked in irony and turns out to be the play's real subject by the third act.

quotations.text: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is To have a thankless child!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: The end of the curse he lays on Goneril, before storming out.
quotations.analysis: He has just asked nature to make her barren, and this is the sentence he finishes on — a father's grievance dressed as a proverb. The comparison is with a bite, which keeps the whole speech inside the play's animal vocabulary, and he leaves the stage without waiting for a reply.

quotations.text: O, reason not the need: our basest beggars Are in the poorest thing superfluous: Allow not nature more than nature needs, Man's life's as cheap as beast's:
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Answering Regan's question, 'What need one?'
quotations.analysis: It is the best argument he makes in the play and he makes it in defence of a hundred armed men he does not need. The reasoning, though, is general and survives the occasion: measure a person by need and you have already agreed they are livestock. Two acts later he applies it to people with no roof at all.

quotations.text: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: His first line on the heath, in the storm.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a line, addressed to weather that cannot obey and does not need to: he is still issuing orders because giving orders is the only register he has. The cheeks belong to the wind-heads on old maps, so the command is aimed at a picture of the world rather than the world.

quotations.text: I am a man More sinn'd against than sinning.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Ending the speech in which he summons hidden criminals to confess.
quotations.analysis: The comparative is doing the pleading: he does not claim innocence, only a favourable balance. It is also the first time in the play he calls himself a man rather than a king, and the sentence is only three words longer than it needs to be because the meter of his self-defence keeps shortening.

quotations.text: Poor naked wretches, whereso'er you are, That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm,
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Outside the hovel, having sent the Fool in first.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence in the play in which he thinks about anyone who is not in the room. He addresses people he cannot see and has never considered, and the admission that follows — that he has taken too little care of this — is the nearest thing to a moral turn the play grants him.

quotations.text: Thou art the thing itself: unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor bare, forked animal as thou art.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Looking at Poor Tom, who is naked in the storm; Lear then starts tearing off his own clothes.
quotations.analysis: It is prose, and the prose matters: the king's verse has gone. 'Forked' is a stage direction as much as an image — two legs, nothing else — and the speech ends not in a conclusion but in an action, which is why the scene is usually remembered as something seen rather than something said.

quotations.text: Lest it see more, prevent it. Out, vile jelly!
quotations.speaker: Cornwall
quotations.context: Putting out Gloucester's second eye, after his own servant has been killed trying to stop him.
quotations.analysis: The reason given is precautionary rather than vengeful, which makes it worse: an eye is destroyed because of what it might otherwise witness. Calling it jelly turns an organ into a substance, and Shakespeare puts the whole thing on stage rather than reporting it, so the audience is made to sit in the room.

quotations.text: I have no way, and therefore want no eyes; I stumbled when I saw:
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Blinded, told by an old tenant that he cannot see his way.
quotations.analysis: 'Want' means lack and need at once, and he uses it to argue himself out of pitying his own condition. The line states the play's central reversal as a plain past tense: the error happened while the eyes were working, so the eyes were never the instrument he needed.

quotations.text: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods. They kill us for their sport.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Spoken to the man he has just hired to lead him, who is his son.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted theology in the play is a man's response to a private disaster, not a conclusion the play endorses; forty lines earlier he was blaming eclipses, and by Act V he dies of joy. Note who hears it: Edgar, in disguise, who could disprove at least part of it by saying his own name.

quotations.text: And the creature run from the cur? There thou mightst behold the great image of authority: a dog's obeyed in office.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Mad, crowned with weeds, talking to the blinded Gloucester in the fields near Dover.
quotations.analysis: Authority is reduced to a reflex in a beggar's legs, and the argument is built from a scene anyone in the audience would have watched in a street. It is prose, spoken by a king who has lost his reason, and it is the most exact political sentence in the play — which is the point of putting it there.

quotations.text: You do me wrong to take me out o' the grave: Thou art a soul in bliss; but I am bound Upon a wheel of fire, that mine own tears Do scald like moulten lead.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Waking in the French camp, seeing Cordelia for the first time since Act I.
quotations.analysis: He wakes into a private hell and assumes his daughter is in heaven, so his first response to rescue is to apologise for being alive near her. The wheel is a torture from an older iconography than this play's Britain, and his own tears are the instrument — nothing is being done to him from outside.

quotations.text: I am a very foolish fond old man, Fourscore and upward, not an hour more nor less; And, to deal plainly, I fear I am not in my perfect mind.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Kneeling to Cordelia, who has told him not to.
quotations.analysis: Three admissions in four lines, each one plainer than anything he has said before: his age, his foolishness, the state of his mind. 'To deal plainly' is the manner he punished Cordelia for in the first scene, and he has arrived at it by way of a heath, a hovel and a field.

quotations.text: Men must endure Their going hence, even as their coming hither; Ripeness is all: come on.
quotations.speaker: Edgar
quotations.context: Getting his father off the battlefield after the British victory.
quotations.analysis: Consolation offered under pressure by a son still refusing to give his name, and it is a stoic commonplace rather than an answer. The last three words undo the grandeur: this is something said to keep a man walking, not a philosophy the play has arrived at.

quotations.text: The wheel is come full circle: I am here.
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: Dying, after Edgar has told him who beat him in the duel.
quotations.analysis: He is the only character in the play to describe his own downfall as a shape, and he sounds almost pleased by the neatness of it. The wheel belongs to Fortune, whose authority he rejected in 1.2 in favour of nature — at the end he accepts the older machinery because it gives his ending a form.

quotations.text: Howl, howl, howl, howl! O, you are men of stones: Had I your tongues and eyes, I'ld use them so That heaven's vault should crack.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Entering with Cordelia dead in his arms.
quotations.analysis: The first word can be an order to the men on stage or a sound he is making himself, and productions have to decide. Either way the line begins outside language, and the accusation that follows — you have tongues and eyes and are not using them — indicts everybody standing there, including the audience.

quotations.text: Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life, And thou no breath at all? Thou'lt come no more, Never, never, never, never, never!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: His last speech, over Cordelia's body.
quotations.analysis: Five stressed nevers make a line of pure trochaic beats, the only one like it in Shakespeare, and it works because the metre has stopped doing anything except repeat. The question before it is the play's animal vocabulary turned inside out: the beasts are alive and the daughter is not, and no account of nature explains it.

timeline.label: The second edition of Holinshed's Chronicles
timeline.detail: Carries the story of King Leir and his three daughters, drawn from Geoffrey of Monmouth, with a restoration that Shakespeare removes.

timeline.label: Sidney's Arcadia
timeline.detail: Supplies the blinded father and the wronged son that Shakespeare builds into the Gloucester plot.

timeline.label: The anonymous King Leir performed
timeline.detail: An older, more openly Christian play on the same story; printed in 1605, and probably known to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: Harsnett's Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures
timeline.detail: The source of the fiends Poor Tom names, and evidence that the play was written after it appeared.

timeline.label: Performed before King James at Whitehall
timeline.detail: The Stationers' Register record and the quarto title page both point to St Stephen's night in the Christmas holidays.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed for Nathaniel Butter as a True Chronicle Historie, and linking the play to the King's Men at the Globe.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1608
timeline.detail: A reprint that keeps the 1608 date on its title page; its true year was not established until the twentieth century.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Printed as The Tragedie of King Lear, with over a hundred lines the quarto lacks and around three hundred fewer of the quarto's.

timeline.label: Nahum Tate's History of King Lear
timeline.detail: Removes the Fool, marries Cordelia to Edgar and lets Lear live. It held the English stage for more than a century.

timeline.label: Macready restores the Fool and the tragic ending
timeline.detail: Priscilla Horton played the restored Fool; Shakespeare's ending returned to public stage memory.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's film
timeline.detail: Made from his 1962 Stratford production, with Paul Scofield as Lear and almost every trace of comfort stripped out.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's RSC production with Ian McKellen
timeline.detail: A stormy, thrust-stage staging that included an on-stage hanging of the Fool.

places.name: Dover
places.note: The cliff Gloucester means to die from, and the coast where Cordelia's army lands.

places.name: Gloucester
places.note: The earldom of the second family, and the title Edmund is given for betraying his father.

places.name: Cornwall
places.note: Regan's dukedom, and the source of the play's most casual cruelty.

places.name: Kent
places.note: The earldom of the man who is banished for honesty in the first scene and comes back disguised.

places.name: Albany
places.note: The old name for the land north of the Forth, and Goneril's husband's title — a duke who slowly changes sides.

places.name: Burgundy
places.note: The suitor who withdraws when Cordelia's dowry disappears, leaving France to take her without one.

criticalViews.position: The play as a Christian pattern of suffering
criticalViews.summary: A long tradition reads Lear's progress as a purgation: pride stripped away by storm and loss until, in 4.7, the king kneels and is reconciled. On this account the tragedy is a form of instruction.
criticalViews.counter: The ending resists it. Cordelia dies after the reprieve has been sent, for no reason the plot requires, and Lear's last words are a demand that four men look at her lips.

criticalViews.position: The play as a political and material tragedy
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the mid-twentieth century has emphasised the play's interest in property, need and power: a division of land, a negotiation over how many servants a pensioner deserves, and a king who works out that office is what makes obedience happen.
criticalViews.counter: It can flatten the family material, which the play stages with as much care as the politics — the arithmetic of 2.4 only devastates because it is done by daughters.

criticalViews.summary: Because the 1608 quarto and the 1623 Folio differ so widely, many textual scholars argue that the Folio represents a later revision and that conflating the two produces a text no early audience heard.
criticalViews.counter: The conflated tradition is what four centuries of readers and actors have worked with, and some of the play's best-known material survives only because editors refused to choose.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use the Gloucester plot?
plan: Set the two opening deceptions side by side: Lear misreads speech in 1.1, Gloucester misreads a document in 1.2.
Distinguish rather than equate — Gloucester's suffering is physical and undeserved by anything he does on stage, Lear's is the consequence of his own ceremony.
Use 3.7 and 4.1 to show the subplot outpacing the main plot: the blinding is the most violent thing in the play and happens to the secondary father.
Analyse 4.6, where the two ruined men meet and the comparison is made on stage instead of by the audience.
Conclude with the endings: Gloucester dies offstage of joy and grief mixed, Lear on stage of neither.

essayQuestions.question: 'The play is about sight, not madness.' Discuss.
plan: Start with Kent's 'See better, Lear' and the eye imagery running through the first scene.
Follow the metaphor into literal action at 3.7, and note what reason Cornwall gives for the second eye.
Read 4.1: Gloucester's claim that he stumbled when he saw, and what it implies about the value of evidence in this play.
Set 4.6 against both — a blind man and a mad king conducting the clearest analysis of authority in the text.
Weigh the counter-case: Lear's madness produces insight that his sanity never did, so the two strands may not be separable.

essayQuestions.question: Are Goneril and Regan given a case?
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, need and the presentation of the sisters
plan: Reconstruct their argument from 1.3, 1.4 and 2.4: a hundred armed men in someone else's house, and a father who curses one daughter with sterility.
Notice how much of their behaviour before 3.7 is administrative rather than cruel, and where exactly the line is crossed.
Use 'O, reason not the need' to show the play answering them at the level of principle rather than fact.
Consider the later plot — the poisoning, the letters to Edmund — and ask whether it convicts them or simply disposes of them.
Decide whether the play gives them a case it then refuses to let them keep.

essayQuestions.question: How far does King Lear offer any consolation?
essayQuestions.focus: The ending, justice and the gods
plan: Collect the appeals to the gods across the play and note that none of them is answered on stage.
Treat 4.7 as the play's best offer: reconciliation, clean clothes, a kneeling king, a daughter who says no cause.
Show how 5.3 dismantles it — the reprieve is sent, and arrives too late by a matter of lines.
Weigh Edgar's 'Ripeness is all' and Albany's closing couplet as attempts to supply a moral that the stage picture contradicts.
Compare Tate's ending, and use it to say precisely what Shakespeare's ending refuses to do.

discussionQuestions: Cordelia could have said something warm and true and kept her third of the kingdom. Why does she not?
The Fool disappears after the mock trial and is never mentioned again. What does the play gain by losing him there?
Edgar keeps his identity from his father for four acts. Is that kindness?
Gloucester says the gods kill us for their sport. Does the play agree with him?
Nahum Tate let Lear live for a hundred and fifty years of English theatre. What exactly does that version lose?

related.why: Written within a year or two, and the other Jacobean tragedy in which a kingdom is described as a body that has gone wrong.
The earlier tragedy of a court that cannot tell performance from feeling, and a hero who tests what others simply believe.
Another play in which a credulous man is talked into destroying the person who loves him, and the machinery is entirely verbal.
A later play about an old ruler, a daughter and the giving up of power, written as though the ending of Lear could be answered.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller material on the quarto and Folio texts, criticism and stage history.
